subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which is the thin, outermost layer of the Earth on which we live?
questions.explain: The crust is the Earth's thin, solid outermost layer, sitting above the mantle.

questions.q: At which type of plate boundary do two plates move apart from each other?
questions.explain: At a constructive boundary plates move apart and rising magma forms new crust.

questions.q: At a destructive plate margin, what happens to the denser oceanic plate where it meets a continental plate?
options: It is subducted beneath the continental plate
It slides sideways past the plate
It splits to form new ocean floor
It is pushed up to form fold mountains
questions.explain: The denser oceanic plate sinks (subducts) beneath the less dense continental plate, forming an ocean trench.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to detect and record the seismic waves produced by an earthquake?
questions.explain: A seismometer records the ground shaking caused by seismic waves during an earthquake.

questions.q: What does the Richter scale measure about an earthquake?
options: The depth of the ocean trench
questions.explain: The Richter scale is a logarithmic measure of an earthquake's magnitude, or the energy it releases.

questions.q: What is the name for the point inside the Earth where an earthquake originates?
questions.explain: The focus is the point underground where the earthquake begins and energy is first released.

questions.q: The epicentre of an earthquake is best described as which of the following?
options: The point on the surface directly above the focus
The deepest point of the earthquake underground
The place where the most aftershocks occur
The boundary between two tectonic plates
questions.explain: The epicentre is the location on the Earth's surface lying directly above the focus.

questions.q: California's San Andreas Fault, where two plates grind past one another, is an example of which margin?
questions.explain: At a conservative margin plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes but no volcanoes, as at the San Andreas Fault.

questions.q: The Himalayas were formed where two continental plates met. Which type of boundary produced them?
options: A subduction zone with oceanic crust
questions.explain: When two continental plates collide, neither subducts easily and the crust is forced upward into fold mountains such as the Himalayas.

questions.q: Roughly what minimum sea-surface temperature is needed for a tropical storm to form?
questions.explain: Tropical storms require warm ocean water of about 27 degrees Celsius to provide the energy and moisture they need.

questions.q: What is the name of the calm, clear area of sinking air at the centre of a tropical storm?
questions.explain: The eye is the calm centre of the storm where air descends, bringing clear, dry conditions.

questions.q: Which part of a tropical storm experiences the strongest winds and heaviest rainfall?
questions.explain: The eye wall, immediately surrounding the eye, has the tallest clouds, strongest winds and heaviest rain.

questions.q: Which scale is used to categorise the strength of a tropical storm (hurricane)?
questions.explain: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from category 1 to 5 based on their sustained wind speeds.

questions.q: Why does a tropical storm usually weaken and die out once it moves over land?
options: It is cut off from the warm ocean water that fuels it
The land heats the storm too strongly
The Coriolis effect stops working on land
Air pressure at the centre suddenly falls
questions.explain: Over land the storm loses its supply of warm, moist ocean air, so it runs out of energy and weakens.

questions.q: A powerful tropical storm develops over the warm waters of the western Pacific Ocean. What name is given to such a storm in this region?
questions.explain: Tropical storms are called typhoons in the western Pacific, hurricanes in the Atlantic and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: Tropical storms typically form between about 5 and 30 degrees north and south of the Equator, but not on the Equator itself. Why not on the Equator?
options: The Coriolis effect is too weak there to make the storm spin
The sea is too warm on the Equator
There is no moisture in equatorial air
Air pressure is too high on the Equator
questions.explain: The Coriolis effect, which makes storms rotate, is negligible at the Equator, so storms cannot spin up there.

questions.q: Designing and constructing earthquake-resistant buildings is an example of which type of hazard-management strategy?
questions.explain: Protection involves modifying buildings and infrastructure so that they can withstand a hazard event.

questions.q: Which technology is most important for predicting the path and arrival of tropical storms so warnings can be issued?
questions.explain: Satellites track developing tropical storms from space, allowing their track and strength to be forecast and warnings to be issued.

questions.q: A country holds regular evacuation drills and stockpiles emergency supplies before its storm season each year. This is an example of which strategy?
questions.explain: Preparation involves planning, drills, education and stockpiling so that people can respond quickly when a hazard strikes.

questions.q: Why do lower-income (developing) countries often suffer higher death tolls from the same tectonic hazard than higher-income countries?
options: They have fewer resources for prediction, protection and preparation
Their earthquakes always have a higher magnitude
They never receive any warning of hazards
They have no tectonic activity to prepare for
questions.explain: Limited money and technology mean weaker buildings, fewer warnings and less effective emergency response, raising the death toll.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Hazardous Environments
